newsitem.title: USA: Sallie Mae votes to privatize under new management.
newsitem.headline: Sallie Mae votes to privatize under new management.

text.p: Student Loan Marketing Association stock owners voted on Thursday to privatise the government-supported enterprise under stewardship of a once-dissident shareholder group.

At a special meeting in Washington, Sallie Mae holders chose a 15-person board of directors comprising members of the Committee to Restore Value, a group that had been dueling for control of the company for several months.

In rejecting a management plan closer to the status quo, stockholders drew praise from Wall Street analysts and saw their shares jump to a 12-month high of $151.50 after the vote. It rose $4.81 to $149.94 in consolidated trading on the New York Stock Exchange.

CRV members had influenced Sallie Mae's business direction for about three years, and Thursday's vote constituted an official endorsement of the group's strategy, said Jonathon Gray, senior research analyst at Sanford C. Bernstein Co.
"This group has shown it's been very sensitive to investment issues," Gray said. "It's been very sensitive to shareholders' interests, and it's shown significant entrepreneurial instincts."
"It is a better group to lead the company into the private sector," he added.

The fully private Sallie Mae will be chaired by Edward Fox, who served as the company's president and chief executive before retiring in 1990. Albert Lord, who sits on the existing Sallie Mae board, will be chief executive, CRV said.

Lord told reporters he hopes to cut Sallie Mae's loan acquisition costs in half. The company buys loans from banks, keeping some for its own portfolio and repackaging the rest for sale to investors. It currently pays a margin of about 2 percent on cash purchases of loans, Lord said.
While Lord called cost-cutting his first priority, he also confirmed that the CRV-run Sallie Mae will for the first time originate loans in addition to purchasing them from lenders.
"I do think we'll be originating at least as many loans as we have planned," he said, referring to already-set lending targets for the future.
Members of the outgoing Sallie Mae board have warned that venturing into lending would place the company at odds with some of its banking clients.
But Thomas O'Donnell, a Smith Barney Inc. analyst of government-sponsored enterprises, said the two objectives reflect different facets of a single strategy.
"I think they're going to originate opportunistically, O'Donnell said. "In places where they're getting good loan production and have good relationships with lenders, they're not going to originate."
Loans issued directly offer 40 percent to 50 percent more profitability than acquired loans, Sanford C. Bernstein's Gray said.
"There's no question the origination of student loans makes a great deal of sense for Sallie Mae," Gray said.
Chairman-elect Fox told reporters the new management team could convene immediately after an official vote tally, expected as soon as Tuesday.
CRV estimated its slate garnered 25.5 million votes and management's received 18.5 million.

The decision to privatise was more lopsided, with about 83 percent of shareholders voting favourably, Sallie Mae officials said. Congress declared in 1996 that Sallie Mae, created by the government in 1972 to provide funding for federal student loans, must privatise or liquidate.
"Sallie Mae shareholders have made their choice regarding the future and direction of Sallie Mae," said outgoing Chairman William Arceneaux.
